mcqs.question: A monitor stops receiving heartbeats from a node for 4 seconds, right at its timeout threshold. What does the missed heartbeat actually prove?
options: That the node has crashed and needs to be evicted immediately
That the node is silent for some reason — a crash, a GC pause, or a network blip all look identical from here
That the network link to the node is definitely down
That the node's process is still running but its disk has failed
mcqs.explanation: A missed heartbeat only proves silence, not its cause — a crash, a GC pause, and a transient network blip are indistinguishable to the monitor at that moment. Assuming any one specific cause (crash, network-only, disk failure) reads more into the signal than it actually carries.

mcqs.question: How does a phi-accrual detector decide when to suspect a node, compared to a fixed-timeout detector?
options: It uses the same fixed timeout as any other detector, just renamed
It waits for a majority of other nodes to vote the node down
It always suspects a node the instant any single heartbeat is late
It computes how statistically unlikely the current silence is given that specific node's own recent heartbeat history
mcqs.explanation: Phi-accrual's distinguishing idea is per-node, history-based suspicion: a node with naturally jittery heartbeats gets more tolerance, one with steady heartbeats gets flagged faster for the same silence. It isn't a renamed fixed timeout, doesn't require voting (that's gossip-based detection), and doesn't fire on a single late beat.

mcqs.question: Why can no failure detector over a truly asynchronous network guarantee both completeness and accuracy?
options: Because any finite timeout can be exceeded by an unbounded message delay, forcing a choice between false positives and slow true-positive detection
Because heartbeats consume too much network bandwidth to run reliably at scale
Because only byzantine failures are theoretically undetectable, and crash failures are always detectable
Because TCP does not support keep-alive packets on all operating systems
mcqs.explanation: The impossibility is structural: since an asynchronous network has no upper bound on delay, any fixed timeout can be exceeded by a message that's merely slow, not lost — so guaranteeing no false suspicions (accuracy) means being willing to wait forever, which breaks completeness. It has nothing to do with bandwidth, TCP keep-alives, or being limited to byzantine failures — it applies to plain crash detection too.

mcqs.question: A company-wide 3-second health-check timeout works fine for most services but keeps falsely evicting a batch worker with a legitimately bursty 5-second p99. What's the right fix?
options: Raise the company-wide default to 5 seconds for every service
Disable health checks entirely for the batch worker
Tune that worker's own timeout (or phi threshold) against its own latency distribution instead of the shared default
Reduce the batch worker's replica count so fewer false evictions occur
mcqs.explanation: A detector should track deviation from a node's own normal, not a one-size-fits-all number — so the fix is a per-service threshold matched to that service's real tail latency. Raising the global default just shifts the mismatch onto latency-sensitive services, disabling checks removes real protection, and replica count doesn't address the timeout mismatch at all.

mcqs.question: Why is a lease-based mechanism safer than a plain failure detector's suspicion for coordinating leader election?
options: A lease requires the leader itself to stop acting when its time window expires, whether or not anyone can confirm why — converting a probabilistic suspicion into a guarantee the old leader has actually stopped
A lease is just a failure detector with a longer timeout, functionally identical otherwise
Leases eliminate the need for any failure detection at all, in every scenario
A lease guarantees a node can never fail, so suspicion becomes unnecessary
mcqs.explanation: The key shift is putting the obligation on the leader to self-evict when its lease lapses, rather than relying on an external, inherently uncertain suspicion — that's what prevents two nodes from both believing they're in charge. It isn't just a renamed timeout, failure detection is still used elsewhere in the system, and leases don't make nodes failure-proof — they bound the damage from failures that do happen.
